issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Rajan is a 64-year-old South Asian man who has been married for nearly four decades and works the early morning shift at a large distribution warehouse on the outskirts of the city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his primary care physician, though he had been carrying what happened to him largely in silence for almost two years.

The event that precipitated his current difficulties occurred during a visit to relatives in a rural area. Rajan was detained overnight by a group of men in what he describes as a partially underground storage structure - dark, earthen-walled, and airless. He was held for approximately eighteen hours, restrained and unable to leave, uncertain whether he would be released or harmed. At some point during the night, he became aware of movement near his feet and realised, in the near-total darkness, that there were snakes in the space with him. He remained motionless for hours, convinced that any movement would provoke a bite. He was eventually released unharmed, but the experience of absolute helplessness - pinned between human threat and animal danger, in the dark, in the early hours before dawn - left a mark that has not faded.

In the months that followed, Rajan found that certain moments in his daily life had become unbearable. The pre-dawn hours of his warehouse shift - the same time of day he had been held - began to feel charged with a formless dread he could not explain to colleagues. Photographs of snakes in a safety pamphlet posted near the loading dock once sent him to the bathroom shaking. Night-time itself, and the simple act of waking in the dark in his own bedroom, had become triggers that pulled him back into the storage room with a vividness he found almost physically painful. These moments of intrusion began to organise his behaviour: he started avoiding sleep, lying awake rather than surrendering to darkness, and when he did sleep, he kept a lamp burning on his side of the bed. He had also begun to check his body obsessively - pressing fingers along his arms and legs each morning, searching for signs of injury or illness he could not rationally account for - and he sought reassurance from his wife and adult children with an urgency that had begun to strain those relationships. His wife, who initially responded with patience, had grown quietly exhausted by his nightly need for confirmation that he was safe.

What Rajan had not anticipated was that the strategies he adopted to manage his distress were themselves keeping him in contact with the very cues he feared. Lying awake in the dark prolonged his exposure to the nighttime environment that triggered the memories; the lamp he kept on created a ritual that marked every night as dangerous, and his body-checking in the early warehouse hours drew his attention precisely to the time-of-day cues he was trying to outlast. The avoidance had become a kind of maintenance.

He had come to believe, with a quiet but settled certainty, that he simply could not cope if the memories were allowed to surface fully - that thinking about what happened would undo him entirely. This conviction sat alongside a deeper fear: that bad things happened to him because he was powerless to prevent them, that the world had shown him something true about his own vulnerability. These appraisals fed directly into his vigilance. Certain that threat could arrive without warning, he had developed a habit of looking behind him on the warehouse floor, scanning the shadows between shelving units, remaining hyperalert throughout his shift in ways that left him exhausted by mid-morning. At night, the same sense of helplessness made it harder to feel safe - the darkness outside his bedroom window seemed less like ordinary night and more like the absence of protection.

There were moments, he admitted, when he was not sure his life was worth continuing. He said this quietly, without drama, as though reporting a weather condition.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a conversation with his youngest son, who had noticed that his father had not slept properly in months and who asked, gently, whether something was wrong. Rajan came to the first session hoping, more than anything, to be able to sleep in the dark again - and to stop feeling, at 64, like a man who had run out of safety.
